Recall that a natural number is a von Neumann natural
([[def-natural-numbers]]): $0 = \varnothing$ and $\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$, so
that

$$n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\} = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$$

is itself the set of its predecessors. Here $<$ is the order of
[[def-nat-order]], which is defined additively, so the displayed identity is a
theorem and not a convention: it is [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]], proved
immediately above. Let $A$ be a set, and let $\approx$ be equinumerosity
([[def-equinumerous]]).

- $A$ is **finite** if $A \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **countably infinite** if $A \approx \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **at most countable** if it is finite or countably infinite.
- $A$ is **uncountable** if it is not at most countable.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. A von Neumann natural is the set of its
predecessors, $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), so it can be
used directly as an index set. Define

$$\mathbb{R}^n := \{\, x : x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\},$$

and write $x_k$ for $x(k)$, $k < n$. Two elements of $\mathbb{R}^n$ are equal
exactly when they agree at every $k < n$, functions being equal when they have
the same values. For $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ put

$$d_1(x,y) := \sum_{k<n} |x_k - y_k|, \qquad d_2(x,y) := \sqrt{\ \sum_{k<n} (x_k - y_k)^2\ }, \qquad d_\infty(x,y) := \max\{\, |x_k - y_k| : k < n \,\}.$$

All three are well defined: the finite sums are those of [[def-finite-sum]]; the
sum of squares is nonnegative ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]], [[lem-of-square-positive]])
so it has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]); and
$\{|x_k - y_k| : k < n\}$ is a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$, because
$n \ge 1$, so it has a maximum ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

**Then $d_1$, $d_2$ and $d_\infty$ are metrics on $\mathbb{R}^n$**
([[def-metric-space]]).

**Why $n \ge 1$.** For $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^0$ has exactly one element,
the empty function, and $d_1$ and $d_2$ are the empty sum $0$ and its root; but
$d_\infty$ would be the maximum of the empty set, which does not exist. The
hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is therefore not decoration, and it is carried by every
statement about $d_\infty$ in this library.

Every Cauchy sequence of reals converges to a real ([[def-real-limit]]).

More carefully, this is a statement about the *axioms*: in a complete ordered
field, that is in an ordered field with the least-upper-bound property
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), every Cauchy sequence converges. The proof
below uses nothing about $\mathbb{R}$ except that property, through
[[thm-bolzano-weierstrass]].

**This library already knows the conclusion by a different route.**
It is proved on the Cauchy-construction page, where
$\mathbb{R}$ is built out of Cauchy sequences of rationals and completeness is
read off the construction. That proof is about a particular construction; this
one is about the axioms, and it is what tells us the statement holds in *any*
complete ordered field, however it was obtained.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) constructed in this
library ([[def-real-numbers]]) and carrying its order ([[def-real-order]]).

Let $X$ be a set. A **metric** on $X$ is a function
$d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x, y, z \in X$:

- **(M1) Separation.** $d(x,y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$.
- **(M2) Symmetry.** $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$.
- **(M3) Triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)$.

A **metric space** is a pair $(X,d)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a metric $d$ on
it. The elements of $X$ are its **points** and $d(x,y)$ is the **distance** from
$x$ to $y$. When only one metric is in play we write $X$ for $(X,d)$; when
several are, the metric is always named.

**The values of a metric are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$d(x,y)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and every
inequality above is an inequality there. No infinite value is permitted;
[[rem-metric-axiom-conventions]] records why extended metrics are not treated in
this library.

**Nonnegativity is deliberately absent from the axiom list.** Many texts add a
fourth axiom $d(x,y) \ge 0$. It is redundant: (M1), (M2) and (M3) already force
it, as [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]] proves. Nothing below assumes it before that
lemma is available.

**Pseudometric.** A **pseudometric** on $X$ is a function
$p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying (M2), (M3) and the weakening

- **(M1') Reflexivity.** $p(x,x) = 0$ for every $x \in X$

of (M1). A pseudometric may therefore assign distance $0$ to two distinct
points. Every metric is a pseudometric, and a pseudometric is a metric exactly
when $p(x,y) = 0$ forces $x = y$.

**Ultrametric.** An **ultrametric** on $X$ is a metric $d$ that in addition
satisfies

- **(M3') Strong triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le \max\{d(x,y), d(y,z)\}$

for all $x, y, z \in X$, where the maximum is that of a two-element subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, which exists and is one of the two elements
([[def-max-min]], [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]). An **ultrametric space** is a pair
$(X,d)$ with $d$ an ultrametric.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

$(X,d)$ is **complete** if every Cauchy sequence in $(X,d)$
([[def-cauchy-in-metric]]) converges to a point of $X$
([[def-metric-convergence]]).

A subset $A \subseteq X$ is called **complete** when the metric subspace
$(A, d_A)$ is complete ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]); as always, the
metric is part of the data, and $d_A$ is the restriction of $d$ to $A \times A$.

**The limit is unique when it exists**, since limits in a metric space are unique
([[lem-metric-limits-unique]]), so a complete space assigns to each of its Cauchy
sequences one point and not a set of points.

**Completeness is a property of the pair $(X,d)$, not of $X$ and not of the
topology of $d$.** Both quantifiers in the definition are about the metric: the
Cauchy condition is stated with distances, and so is convergence. Two metrics on
the same set can have the same open sets while exactly one of them is complete,
which is the content of [[fs-completeness-is-a-topological-property]] and its
witness. Read the word *complete* as an abbreviation for *complete with respect
to this metric*, always.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $(x_k)$ be a
sequence in $X$, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$ written $x_k := x(k)$
([[def-metric-convergence]], [[def-sequence]]). As everywhere in this library
$\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, so a sequence is indexed from $0$.

$(x_k)$ is a **Cauchy sequence in $(X,d)$** if for every rational
$\varepsilon > 0$ there is $K \in \mathbb{N}$ such that

$$d(x_m, x_n) < \varepsilon \qquad \text{for all } m, n \ge K .$$

**Rational and real $\varepsilon$ agree here.** The test is written with a
rational $\varepsilon$ to match [[def-real-limit]] and [[def-metric-convergence]],
and nothing is lost by using a real one: below any real $\eta > 0$ lies a
positive rational ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]), and the index belonging to that
rational serves for $\eta$. So a proof may establish Cauchyness by producing an
index for every real $\varepsilon > 0$, and may use a Cauchy hypothesis at a real
$\varepsilon$ by first passing to a rational below it. Both moves are used on
this page and are always cited.

**The condition is exactly $d(x_m,x_n) \to 0$ as $m$ and $n$ grow
independently.** The distances $d(x_m,x_n)$ are nonnegative reals
([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]), and the displayed condition asks them to be
uniformly small on a tail of the doubly indexed family. It is not the same as
$d(x_{k+1}, x_k) \to 0$, which is a strictly weaker condition and is a standing
source of error. The partial sums $H_n$ of the harmonic series separate the two:
consecutive ones differ by $1/(n+1)$, which tends to $0$, while the sequence is
unbounded, and an unbounded sequence of reals is not Cauchy
([[lem-metric-cauchy-bounded]]).

**Consistency with the real line.** For $X = \mathbb{R}$ with the usual metric
$d(x,y) = |x-y|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) the condition above reads
$|x_m - x_n| < \varepsilon$ for $m,n \ge K$, which is verbatim the definition of a
Cauchy sequence of reals ([[def-real-limit]]). So the notion introduced here
restricts on $\mathbb{R}$ to the one already in use, and no ambiguity is created.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

A **sequence in $X$** is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$, written $(x_k)$ with
$x_k := x(k)$. As everywhere in this library, $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$
([[def-natural-numbers]]) and a sequence is indexed from $0$
([[def-sequence]]); an index range copied from a text that starts at $1$ must be
shifted before it is used here.

Let $(x_k)$ be a sequence in $X$ and $p \in X$. The function
$k \mapsto d(x_k, p)$ is a sequence of reals ([[def-sequence]]), and it is
nonnegative ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]), so $|d(x_k,p)| = d(x_k,p)$
([[def-abs-value]]). Define

$$x_k \longrightarrow p \text{ in } (X,d) \quad :\Longleftrightarrow \quad d(x_k,p) \longrightarrow 0 \text{ in } \mathbb{R},$$

the convergence on the right being that of [[def-real-limit]]. Unwound, this
says: for every **rational** $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $K \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$d(x_k, p) < \varepsilon$ for every $k \ge K$. We then call $p$ a **limit** of
$(x_k)$, and say $(x_k)$ **converges** in $(X,d)$ if it has a limit.

**Rational and real $\varepsilon$ agree here, as they do on the real line.**
[[def-real-limit]] tests convergence against rational $\varepsilon$ only, and its
own remark, restated for sequences in [[def-sequence]], records that nothing is
lost: below any real $\eta > 0$ lies a positive rational
([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]), and the index belonging to that rational serves for
$\eta$. So a proof may establish convergence by producing an index for every
real $\varepsilon > 0$, and may use a convergence hypothesis at a real
$\varepsilon$ by first passing to a rational below it. Both moves are used on
this page and are always cited.

**Subsequences and subsequential limits.** A **subsequence** of $(x_k)$ is the
composite $x \circ n$ for a strictly increasing $n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$,
written $(x_{n_j})$, exactly as for sequences of reals ([[def-sequence]]); and
$p$ is a **subsequential limit** of $(x_k)$ in $(X,d)$ when some subsequence
converges to $p$, which is the metric-space form of [[def-subsequential-limit]].

A sequence $(x_k)$ of reals **converges** to $x \in \mathbb{R}$ when for
every rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $K$ with
$|x_k - x| < \hat\varepsilon$ for all $k \ge K$. It is **Cauchy** when for
every rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $K$ with
$|x_k - x_l| < \hat\varepsilon$ for all $k, l \ge K$.

Let $(x_k)$ be a sequence of reals ([[def-sequence]]) and let $x, y \in
\mathbb{R}$. If $(x_k)$ converges to $x$ and $(x_k)$ converges to $y$
([[def-real-limit]]), then $x = y$. A sequence therefore has at most one limit,
and when a limit exists it may be denoted $\lim_{k} x_k$.
Every nonempty subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has a least element: there is $\ell \in S$ with $\ell \le s$ for all $s \in S$.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.
The relation $\le$ on $\mathbb{N}$, where $m \le n \iff \exists k\ (m + k = n)$ ([[def-nat-order]]), is a linear (total) order: reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive, and total.

derivations.claim: If $S=\emptyset$, then $B(S)$ has exactly one element, the empty function. Its only distance is $0$; nonnegativity, symmetry, separation, and the triangle inequality all hold on this singleton, and every sequence in it is constant and convergent.

Suppose $S\ne\emptyset$. By [F1], fix $n\ge1$ and a bijection $e:n\to S$. Pulling functions back along $e$ identifies $B(S)$ with $\mathbb R^n$ and carries $d_\infty$ exactly to the max metric of [F2]; hence it is a metric.

Let $(U_m)$ be Cauchy in $d_\infty$ on $B(S)$. For each $j<n$, define the real sequence $x^{(j)}_m:=U_m(e(j))$. Given rational $\varepsilon>0$, the metric Cauchy condition supplies $K$ such that $d_\infty(U_m,U_\ell)<\varepsilon$ for all $m,\ell\ge K$. Since the pulled-back $d_\infty$ is the maximum of the coordinate differences, $|x^{(j)}_m-x^{(j)}_\ell|<\varepsilon$ for every $j<n$ and $m,\ell\ge K$. Thus each coordinate sequence is Cauchy in $\mathbb R$.
By [F3], each coordinate sequence converges. Denote its unique limit by $y_j\in\mathbb R$, using [F6].
Define $U:S\to\mathbb R$ by $U(e(j)):=y_j$ for $j<n$. This is well defined because $e$ is a bijection, and it uses no choice because every $y_j$ is uniquely determined.

Fix rational $\varepsilon>0$. For each $j<n$, convergence to $y_j$ gives a nonempty set of natural thresholds $K$ such that $|x^{(j)}_m-y_j|<\varepsilon$ for all $m\ge K$. Let $K_j$ be its least member, using [F7].

The finite nonempty list $K_0,\ldots,K_{n-1}$ has a maximum $K$: start with $K_0$ and, at each successor, retain the larger of the current maximum and the next threshold, which exists by the total order on $\mathbb N$; induction proves the resulting value dominates every entry. Thus $K\ge K_j$ for all $j<n$.

For every $m\ge K$, step 5.1 implies $|U_m(e(j))-U(e(j))|<\varepsilon$ for every $j<n$. Their finite maximum is one of these coordinate differences, so $d_\infty(U_m,U)<\varepsilon$. Since this holds for every rational $\varepsilon>0$, $(U_m)$ converges to $U$ in $d_\infty$. Every Cauchy sequence therefore converges in $B(S)$, and together with the metric property from steps 1.1–1.2 this proves completeness.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. In every bounded-reward finite discounted Markov decision process with nonempty finite state set $S$, nonempty finite action sets $A(s)$, and $0\le\gamma<1$, the trajectory law of every history-dependent behavior from every starting state exists. Its discounted return is measurable, integrable, and between $0$ and $1/(1-\gamma)$. For each stationary policy $\pi$, its value $V^\pi$ satisfies its Bellman equation. The optimality operator

$$T^*V(s)=\max_{a\in A(s)}\left[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)V(s')\right]$$

is a $\gamma$ contraction in the supremum norm, meaning $\|T^*V-T^*W\|_\infty\le\gamma\|V-W\|_\infty$ for all $V,W:S\to\mathbb R$, where $\|V\|_\infty=\max_{s\in S}|V(s)|$, and has a unique fixed point $V^*$. This fixed point is the supremum of the values of all history-dependent behaviors and is attained by a deterministic stationary greedy policy. The optimal action value is

$$Q^*(s,a)=r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)V^*(s'),$$

and $V^*(s)=\max_{a\in A(s)}Q^*(s,a)$ with $Q^*(s,a)\ge0$.

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and all $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{R}$, the
set $\{a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ has a maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]).

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$.

The usual reading, that *every nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has a
maximum and a minimum*, follows once one identifies the nonempty finite subsets
of $\mathbb{R}$ with the sets listable as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$. That
identification is recorded as a stipulation in the Given below, because this page
has no definition of finiteness to prove it against. **It is discharged, not
merely assumed**: [[lem-finite-subsets-listable]] proves that the two
descriptions of a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ agree. That lemma is
recorded in `justified_by` rather than in `deps`, since it is about the sets this
lemma quantifies over and therefore depends on this one. This is what licenses
the notation
$\max\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ and $\min\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ for finite sets of
**real** numbers from this page onwards.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

Let $S$ be a nonempty finite set, let $A(s)$ be a nonempty finite set for each $s\in S$, and let $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$. Here **finite** means bijective with a natural number. Put $S_0=|S|$ and $A_0=\max_{s\in S}|A(s)|$. Fix a discount $0\le\gamma<1$. Give $S$ and $D$ their discrete sigma-algebras and give $[0,1]$ its Borel sigma-algebra. A **bounded-reward finite discounted Markov decision process** is a probability kernel $K$ from $D$ to $S\times[0,1]$. At pair $(s,a)$, $K(\cdot\mid s,a)$ is the joint law of the next state and the reward; these two coordinates need not be independent. Define the state-transition probabilities and expected rewards by

$$P(s'\mid s,a)=K(\{s'\}\times[0,1]\mid s,a),\qquad r(s,a)=\int_{S\times[0,1]}\rho\,K(ds',d\rho\mid s,a).$$

A **history-dependent behavior** is a sequence of probability kernels from observed-history spaces $H_t$ to the finite action alphabet $\mathcal A=\bigcup_{s\in S}A(s)$, assigning probability zero to actions outside $A(s_t)$ at every history ending in state $s_t$. Here $H_t$ consists of histories $(s_0,a_0,R_1,s_1,\ldots,a_{t-1},R_t,s_t)$, with discrete sigma-algebras on finite state/action coordinates and the Borel sigma-algebra on each reward coordinate; it has the resulting finite-product sigma-algebra. A **stationary Markov policy** assigns one distribution on $A(s)$ to each state, independently of earlier history. During interaction, after choosing $a_t$ in state $s_t$, the next pair $(s_{t+1},R_{t+1})$ is drawn from $K(\cdot\mid s_t,a_t)$.

derivations.claim: Fix a stationary policy $\pi$ and put $d=\|V_1^\pi-V_2^\pi\|_\infty$. Subtract its two Bellman equations. For each state, split the transition term as $P_1(V_1^\pi-V_2^\pi)+(P_1-P_2)V_2^\pi$. The first part has absolute value at most $d$ because $P_1$ is a probability vector; the second is at most $V\|P_1-P_2\|_1\le V\beta$ because $0\le V_2^\pi\le V$. Averaging over the common policy's action distribution and using the reward error gives $|V_1^\pi(s)-V_2^\pi(s)|\le\alpha+\gamma d+\gamma V\beta$. Taking the maximum over states and rearranging yields the first bound.

Put $d=\|V_1^*-V_2^*\|_\infty$. For any state and action, the two optimal Bellman backup entries differ by at most $\alpha+\gamma d+\gamma V\beta$, by the same transition splitting and the cap on $V_2^*$. For finite lists $(x_a),(y_a)$, $|\max_a x_a-\max_a y_a|\le\max_a|x_a-y_a|$: each $x_a\le y_a+m$ and $y_a\le x_a+m$ for $m=\max_a|x_a-y_a|$. Thus the optimal Bellman equations in [F1] imply $d\le\alpha+\gamma d+\gamma V\beta$. Rearranging proves the second bound.

Under the additional trap-model hypotheses, fix $\pi$ and put $d=\|V_1^\pi-V_2^\pi\|_\infty$. Bellman subtraction as in step 1.1 gives $d\le\alpha+\gamma d+\gamma\beta\|V_2^\pi\|_\infty$. By [A1] and the triangle inequality, $\|V_2^\pi\|_\infty\le\|V_1^\pi\|_\infty+d\le2W+d$. Hence $(1-\gamma-\gamma\beta)d\le\alpha+2\gamma W\beta$. Since $\gamma\beta\le(1-\gamma)/2$, the left coefficient is at least $(1-\gamma)/2$, yielding $d\le2(\alpha+2\gamma W\beta)/(1-\gamma)$.

For optimal values, use the finite-maximum inequality from step 1.2 in the Bellman subtraction. It gives $d=\|V_1^*-V_2^*\|_\infty\le\alpha+\gamma d+\gamma\beta\|V_2^*\|_\infty$. Again [A1] and the triangle inequality give $\|V_2^*\|_\infty\le2W+d$. The same rearrangement as step 2.1 proves the optimal-value bound.

Assume AC and fix a bounded-reward finite discounted MDP with state set $S$. For each admissible pair $(s,a)$, let $(S'_i,R_i)_{i\ge1}$ be an independent potential stream with common joint law $K(\cdot\mid s,a)$; an interaction reveals the next unused sample from that pair's stream only when the pair is visited. This construction has the same finite-trajectory law as interaction with the MDP under any history-dependent behavior. For a fixed pair and $m\ge1$, its reward samples satisfy
$$\mathbb P\!\left(\left|\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m R_i-r(s,a)\right|>x\right)\le 2e^{-2mx^2}\qquad(x>0).$$
If $\widehat P_m$ is the empirical distribution of $S'_1,\ldots,S'_m$ and $P(\cdot\mid s,a)$ is the true next-state marginal, then
$$\mathbb E\|\widehat P_m-P(\cdot\mid s,a)\|_1\le\sqrt{\frac{|S|}{m}},\qquad \mathbb P\!\left(\|\widehat P_m-P(\cdot\mid s,a)\|_1>\sqrt{\frac{|S|}{m}}+\sqrt{\frac{2\ln(1/\delta)}{m}}\right)\le\delta\quad(0<\delta<1),$$
where $\|q\|_1=\sum_{s'\in S}|q(s')|$ and $\ln$ is the natural logarithm.
More generally, for a filtration $(\mathcal F_i)_{i=0}^m$, if $Y_i$ is $\mathcal F_i$-measurable, $0\le Y_i\le B$, and $\mu_i=\mathbb E[Y_i\mid\mathcal F_{i-1}]$, then
$$\mathbb P\!\left(\left|\sum_{i=1}^m(Y_i-\mu_i)\right|\ge mx\right)\le2e^{-2mx^2/B^2}\qquad(B>0,\ x>0).$$
No independence between reward and next state within a single transition is assumed. The confidence bounds are for a fixed deterministic sample size or a fixed-size batch; this item makes no uniform confidence claim at a data-dependent sample count. At a finite history-dependent visit count, the next fixed number of unused potential outcomes still has its conditional iid law.

Let $M_1$ and $M_2$ be bounded-reward finite discounted MDPs on the same finite state set $S$ and the same admissible action sets, with common discount $0\le\gamma<1$. Write $r_i,P_i,V_i^\pi,V_i^*$ for their mean rewards, transition laws, stationary-policy values, and optimal values. Suppose $0\le V_i^\pi(s),V_i^*(s)\le V$ for every state, model index $i$, and stationary policy $\pi$, and that for every admissible pair
$$|r_1(s,a)-r_2(s,a)|\le\alpha,\qquad \|P_1(\cdot\mid s,a)-P_2(\cdot\mid s,a)\|_1\le\beta.$$
For finite vectors, $\|v\|_\infty=\max_{s\in S}|v(s)|$ and $\|p\|_1=\sum_{s\in S}|p(s)|$.
Then every common stationary policy and the optimal values satisfy
$$\|V_1^\pi-V_2^\pi\|_\infty\le\frac{\alpha+\gamma V\beta}{1-\gamma},\qquad \|V_1^*-V_2^*\|_\infty\le\frac{\alpha+\gamma V\beta}{1-\gamma}.$$
There is also a trap-model form that does not assume a tight cap for the second model: for $W>0$, suppose all stationary-policy and optimal values in $M_1$ are at most $2W$, all rewards in $M_2$ lie in $[0,1]$, and $\gamma\beta\le(1-\gamma)/2$. Then every common stationary policy and the optimal values satisfy
$$\|V_1^\pi-V_2^\pi\|_\infty\le\frac{2(\alpha+2\gamma W\beta)}{1-\gamma},\qquad \|V_1^*-V_2^*\|_\infty\le\frac{2(\alpha+2\gamma W\beta)}{1-\gamma}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. In every bounded-reward finite discounted Markov decision process with nonempty finite state set $S$, nonempty finite action sets $A(s)$, and $0\le\gamma<1$, the trajectory law of every history-dependent behavior from every starting state exists. Its discounted return is measurable, integrable, and between $0$ and $1/(1-\gamma)$. For each stationary policy $\pi$, its value $V^\pi$ satisfies its Bellman equation. The optimality operator

$$T^*V(s)=\max_{a\in A(s)}\left[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)V(s')\right]$$

is a $\gamma$ contraction in the supremum norm, meaning $\|T^*V-T^*W\|_\infty\le\gamma\|V-W\|_\infty$ for all $V,W:S\to\mathbb R$, where $\|V\|_\infty=\max_{s\in S}|V(s)|$, and has a unique fixed point $V^*$. This fixed point is the supremum of the values of all history-dependent behaviors and is attained by a deterministic stationary greedy policy. The optimal action value is

$$Q^*(s,a)=r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)V^*(s'),$$

and $V^*(s)=\max_{a\in A(s)}Q^*(s,a)$ with $Q^*(s,a)\ge0$.

For a bounded-reward finite discounted MDP, an **admissible upper heuristic** is a function $U:D\to[0,V_0]$ such that $Q^*(s,a)\le U(s,a)$ for every admissible pair and a supplied scalar satisfies $0\le V_0\le(1-\gamma)^{-1}$. Define the effective reward-scale cap $V_{\max}=\max\{1,V_0\}$. Then $U(s,a)\le V_{\max}\le(1-\gamma)^{-1}$. The floor at $1$ is part of this convention because an observed reward can lie anywhere in $[0,1]$, even when the heuristic values are all smaller than $1$.

Let $M$ be a bounded-reward finite discounted MDP with discount $\gamma$, let $K\subseteq D$ be a set of known state-action pairs, and let $q:D\to[0,V_{\max}]$ with $V_{\max}\le(1-\gamma)^{-1}$. The **known-state/action MDP** $M_K(q)$ agrees with $M$ on every pair in $K$. For each pair $(s,a)\notin K$, add a distinct absorbing state $\bot_{s,a}$ with one admissible action. The unknown pair transitions deterministically to $\bot_{s,a}$ and gives deterministic reward $(1-\gamma)q(s,a)$; the sink action self-loops with the same deterministic reward $(1-\gamma)q(s,a)$. These rewards lie in $[0,1]$. The sink state's value is $q(s,a)$, so the unknown pair's Bellman backup is exactly $(1-\gamma)q(s,a)+\gamma q(s,a)=q(s,a)$, independent of the value function on the original states.

**Input:** A bounded-reward finite discounted MDP interaction, its discount $0\le\gamma<1$, an admissible upper heuristic $U$ with cap $V_{\max}$, an integer sample threshold $m\ge1$, a value-iteration error tolerance $0<\beta<(1-\gamma)^{-1}$, and a fixed total order on each finite action set. Write $\ln$ for the natural logarithm.

**Output:** At each interaction time $t$, the selected action $a_t$. The action-value table $Q$, known set, sample lists, and empirical model are internal state; the procedure does not return $Q$ as an output.

Initialize each pair as unknown, set $Q(s,a)=U(s,a)$, and give each pair an empty list of observed rewards and next states. For interaction times $t=1,2,\ldots$, in the current state choose a maximizing action using the fixed tie order, output and take that action $a_t$, and observe reward $R_{t+1}$ and next state $S_{t+1}$. If the pair is unknown, append this observation until its list has length $m$. When it reaches $m$, mark the pair known, set its empirical reward to the sample mean and its empirical transition law to the sample frequencies. Rebuild all action values by setting the working table $Q^{(0)}(s,a)=0$, then for $j=0,\ldots,L-1$ setting $Q^{(j+1)}=H_KQ^{(j)}$, and finally replacing $Q$ by $Q^{(L)}$, for the operator
$$H_KQ(s,a)=\begin{cases}\widehat r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}\widehat P(s'\mid s,a)\max_{b\in A(s')}Q(s',b),&(s,a)\in K,\\ U(s,a),&(s,a)\notin K,\end{cases}$$
where $K$ is the current known set and
$$L=\max\!\left\{1,\left\lceil\frac{\ln(1/[\beta(1-\gamma)])}{1-\gamma}\right\rceil\right\}.$$
Pairs and their samples are never removed from $K$ or discarded. After processing the observation and any rebuild, use the observed $S_{t+1}$ as the current state in the next iteration. The algorithm specifies no computational-time bound.

For every finite family of events $A_0,\ldots,A_{n-1}$,
$$\mathbb P\!\left(\bigcup_{i<n}A_i\right)\le\sum_{i<n}\mathbb P(A_i).$$
For $n=0$ both sides are $0$.

derivations.claim: Apply [F1] to each pair with reward and transition tolerance $b$. For $\delta_0=\delta/(4SA)$, the transition threshold is $\sqrt{S/m}+\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta_0)/m}\le b$: its squared numerator is at most $2S+4\ln(1/\delta_0)\le4(S+L_0)$, while $m\ge8(S+L_0)/b^2$. The reward failure is at most $2e^{-2mb^2}\le\delta_0$ because $2mb^2\ge16(S+L_0)\ge\ln(2/\delta_0)$. By [F6], the finite union over reward and transition events for at most $SA$ pairs has failure probability at most $2SA\delta_0=\delta/2$.

The Bellman operator of $\widehat M_K$ is exactly the operator in [F5], with unknown backup $U$. Its fixed point and zero-initialized sweeps lie in $[0,(1-\gamma)^{-1}]$. The contraction estimate in [F3] gives error at most $\gamma^L/(1-\gamma)$. For $0<\gamma<1$, $\ln\gamma\le-(1-\gamma)$, so the stated $L$ makes this error at most $\beta$; when $\gamma=0$, one sweep is exact. The initial table $U$ is the exact fixed point for the empty known set. Thus the action-value approximation bound holds after every rebuild.

For a fixed known set $K$, the true trap model has every stationary-policy and optimal value at most $2V_{\max}$. Indeed, until the first outside-$K$ pair its path is a true-MDP path, whose expected nonnegative prefix is at most $V^*(s)\le V_{\max}$; after that pair its absorbing continuation is at most $U(s,a)\le V_{\max}$. The empirical trap model has all rewards in $[0,1]$. Also $\gamma b\le(1-\gamma)/2$, since $\gamma b/(1-\gamma)=\gamma\eta/(64V_{\max})<1/256$. Apply the trap-model form of [F2] with $W=V_{\max}$ and $\alpha=\beta=b$. The value error for each policy and the optimum is at most $2b(1+2\gamma V_{\max})/(1-\gamma)=\eta(1+2\gamma V_{\max})/(32V_{\max})\le3\eta/32<\eta/8$.

Let $V^*_{M_K}$ and $V^*_{\widehat M_K}$ denote the trap-model optima. For every state, the true Bellman backup at $V^*$ on a known pair is $Q^*(s,a)$, and on an unknown pair the trap backup is $U(s,a)\ge Q^*(s,a)$. Hence $T_{M_K}^*V^*\ge V^*$. The operator preserves coordinatewise order because its transition weights are nonnegative; its iterates from $V^*$ therefore increase. Contraction makes these iterates converge to the unique fixed point, so $V^*_{M_K}\ge V^*$. Step 2.1 gives $V^*_{\widehat M_K}\ge V^*_{M_K}-\eta/8$. Since $\|Q_t-Q^*_{\widehat M_K}\|_\infty\le\beta$, $V_t\ge V^*_{\widehat M_K}-\beta\ge V^*-(\eta/8+\beta)\ge V^*-\eta$.

For each state $s$, the action chosen by $\pi_t$ satisfies $Q^*_{\widehat M_K}(s,\pi_t(s))\ge V^*_{\widehat M_K}(s)-2\beta$: its optimal action value is at least its estimated value minus $\beta$, while the estimated maximum is at least the optimal maximum minus $\beta$. Thus $T^{\pi_t}_{\widehat M_K}V^*_{\widehat M_K}\ge V^*_{\widehat M_K}-2\beta$. Subtracting the policy Bellman equation and taking the maximum positive difference yields $V^*_{\widehat M_K}-V^{\pi_t}_{\widehat M_K}\le2\beta/(1-\gamma)$. Comparing the same policy in $M_K$ by step 2.1 and using $V_t\le V^*_{\widehat M_K}+\beta$ gives $V_t-V^{\pi_t}_{M_K}\le\beta+2\beta/(1-\gamma)+\eta/8\le5\eta/16<\eta$, because $\beta=\eta(1-\gamma)/16$.

On the event just proved, an outside-$K_t$ pair with $U(s,a)<V^*(s)-\eta$ cannot be selected: its current value is still $Q_t(s,a)=U(s,a)$, whereas $V_t(s)\ge V^*(s)-\eta$. Thus every escape pair lies in $E_\eta$. By [F5], each such pair is selected outside the known set at most $m$ times and causes one rebuild. Summing over $E_\eta$ proves the complexity bound.

citations.quote: Let $S$ be a finite nonempty state set and let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty action set for each $s\in S$, as in the finite-MDP convention. Put $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$ with its discrete sigma-algebra. Equip $S$ with its power-set sigma-algebra, $[0,1]$ with its Borel sigma-algebra, and $S\times[0,1]$ with the product sigma-algebra. A finite MDP with bounded real rewards specifies a probability kernel $Q$ from $D$ to $S\times[0,1]$; equivalently, each admissible $(s,a)$ has a probability measure $Q(\cdot\mid s,a)$ on that product measurable space. The reward-coordinate projection $(s',\rho)\mapsto\rho$ is measurable because the preimage of each Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$ is the product rectangle $S\times B$. Define the next-state law by $P(s'\mid s,a)=Q(\{s'\}\times[0,1]\mid s,a)$ and the mean reward by $r(s,a)=\int_{S\times[0,1]}\rho\,Q(ds',d\rho\mid s,a)\in[0,1]$. At each time, conditional on the observed history and the selected action, the next-state/reward pair has this law. Assume the Axiom of Choice for the path-space construction under policies.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the path-space construction. Fix a finite-horizon interaction of length $T$ in a finite MDP with bounded rewards and any nonanticipating policy: each action distribution is a measurable function of the revealed history, and policy randomization is independent of unexposed MDP samples. On an enlarged probability space with the same law for the observed interaction, for each admissible pair $(s,a)$ there is a sequence $Z_{s,a,1},\ldots,Z_{s,a,T}$ of independent samples with common law $Q(\cdot\mid s,a)$ such that the $j$th observed next-state/reward pair at $(s,a)$ is $Z_{s,a,j}$ whenever that visit occurs.

Assume AC. Let $(M_k,\mathcal F_k)_{k=0}^n$ be a martingale. Suppose finite $\mathcal F_{k-1}$-measurable $A_k,B_k$ and deterministic $c_k\ge0$ satisfy
$$A_k\le M_k-M_{k-1}\le B_k,\qquad B_k-A_k\le c_k$$
almost surely. Then for every $t>0$,
$$\mathbb P(M_n-M_0\ge t)\le \exp\!\left(-\frac{2t^2}{\sum_{k=1}^n c_k^2}\right),$$
and the analogous lower-tail bound holds, with the zero-denominator expression interpreted as $0$.

Assume AC [[def-axiom-of-choice]] for conditional-expectation existence. A **martingale difference sequence** relative to $(\mathcal F_n)_{n\ge0}$ is a sequence $(D_n)_{n\ge1}$ of real integrable variables such that $D_n$ is $\mathcal F_n$-measurable and
$$E[D_n\mid\mathcal F_{n-1}]=0\quad\text{a.s. for every }n\ge1.$$
Integrability and adaptedness have the timewise meanings of [[def-adapted-and-integrable-stochastic-process]]. Conditional expectations have the class convention of [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]], which is the exact inherited use of AC here. No representative is selected by this definition. There is no $D_0$, and $\mathcal F_0$ need not be trivial or generated by the differences.

Assume AC. If $M$ is a martingale, then $D_n=M_n-M_{n-1}$, $n\ge1$, is a martingale difference sequence. Conversely, given a martingale difference sequence $D$ and any integrable $\mathcal F_0$-measurable real $M_0$, the process $M_n=M_0+\sum_{k=1}^nD_k$ is a martingale. For fixed $M_0$ these constructions are inverse.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: By [F2], each pair's observed samples are prefixes of a fixed i.i.d. tape with law $Q(\cdot\mid s,a)$. By [F1], its reward coordinate has mean $r(s,a)$ and its next-state coordinate has law $P(\cdot\mid s,a)$. Rewards and indicators of next-state subsets lie in $[0,1]$. The finite tape construction uses AC exactly as stated in [A1].

By [F4] and [F5], the centered reward tape prefix has martingale partial sums with width-one increments; applying [F3] to that sum and to its negative gives the two-sided prefix tail $2e^{-2n\varepsilon^2}$. For a fixed pair and $n$, set $\varepsilon_r=\sqrt{7\log(4SAT/\delta)/(2n)}$. Step 1.1 bounds the failure probability by $2(\delta/(4SAT))^7$. Union over at most $SA$ pairs and $T$ possible prefix lengths gives at most $2SAT(\delta/(4SAT))^7\le\delta/2$.

For transition observations, fix a subset $B\subseteq S$. By step 1.1, the indicators $\mathbf1_{\{S'\in B\}}$ have mean $P(B\mid s,a)$ and range $[0,1]$. Their centered tape coordinates satisfy [F4]; by [F5] their partial sums are martingales, so [F3] gives $2e^{-2n u^2}$ for a deviation larger than $u$. For two probability vectors $p,q$ on a finite set, $\|p-q\|_1=2\max_{B\subseteq S}|p(B)-q(B)|$: the positive coordinates of $p-q$ sum to half its $\ell^1$ norm, and choosing exactly those coordinates attains the maximum. Therefore an $\ell^1$ deviation larger than $\varepsilon$ implies that some subset indicator deviates by more than $\varepsilon/2$. A union bound over the $2^S$ subsets gives $2^{S+1}e^{-n\varepsilon^2/2}$.

Set $L=\log(4AT/\delta)$ and $\varepsilon_p=\sqrt{14S L/n}$. Step 2.2 gives per-pair, per-prefix failure probability at most $2^{S+1}e^{-7SL}$. Union over at most $SAT$ pairs and prefixes is at most $SAT2^{S+1}e^{-7SL}\le\delta/2$: after dividing by $\delta/2$, its logarithm is $\log S+L+S\log2-7SL\le(2S)L-7SL\le0$, using $S\le2^{S-1}$ and $L\ge\log2$. Combining the reward failure bound from step 2.1 with the transition bound just obtained proves the simultaneous claim.

Let $S$ be a finite set, possibly empty, let $\mathcal R$ be a finite subset of $\mathbb R$, and for each $s\in S$ let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty set. Here **finite** means bijective with a natural number, and the **discrete sigma-algebra** on a set is its power set. Write $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$. A **finite Markov decision process (MDP)** consists of these sets and numbers $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)\in[0,1]$, indexed by $(s,a)\in D$, $s'\in S$, and $\rho\in\mathcal R$, with

$$ \sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)=1 \qquad ((s,a)\in D). $$

Equip each set used here, including $D$, with its power-set (discrete) sigma-algebra. Thus $p$ is the point-mass form of a probability kernel from $D$ to $S\times\mathcal R$: each input assigns a probability measure on $S\times\mathcal R$, and every event section is measurable. The joint law allows the next state and reward to be dependent. Define the expected reward and state-transition probabilities by

$$ r(s,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\rho\,p(s',\rho\mid s,a), \qquad P(s'\mid s,a)=\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a). $$

If $\mathcal R\ne\emptyset$, put $M=\max_{\rho\in\mathcal R}|\rho|$; if $\mathcal R=\emptyset$, put $M=0$. A stationary Markov policy is a family of probabilities $\pi(a\mid s)\ge0$ with $\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)=1$ for every $s\in S$. A deterministic policy is a function $\pi$ with $\pi(s)\in A(s)$ for every $s$. When $S=\emptyset$, these families and policies are the unique empty functions and all statewise formulas are vacuous.

For a finite MDP, a discount $0\le\gamma<1$, and a stationary Markov policy $\pi$, define the **policy Bellman operator** $T^\pi:\mathbb R^S\to\mathbb R^S$ by

$$ (T^\pi V)(s)=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)\left[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)V(s')\right]\qquad(s\in S). $$

If $S=\emptyset$, this is the unique map from $\mathbb R^S$ to itself.

For a finite MDP and a discount $0\le\gamma<1$, define the **Bellman optimality operator** $T^*:\mathbb R^S\to\mathbb R^S$ by

$$ (T^*V)(s)=\max_{a\in A(s)}\left[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)V(s')\right]\qquad(s\in S). $$

The maximum exists because each $A(s)$ is finite and nonempty. If $S=\emptyset$, this is the unique map from $\mathbb R^S$ to itself.

For any finite set $S$, let $B(S)=\mathbb R^S$, the set of real-valued functions on $S$. Define

$$ d_\infty(U,V)=\begin{cases}0,&S=\emptyset,\\ \max_{s\in S}|U(s)-V(s)|,&S\ne\emptyset.\end{cases} $$

Then $d_\infty$ is a metric on $B(S)$ and $(B(S),d_\infty)$ is complete.

Put $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$ with its discrete sigma-algebra. Equip $S$ with its power-set sigma-algebra, $[0,1]$ with its Borel sigma-algebra, and $S\times[0,1]$ with the product sigma-algebra. A finite MDP with bounded real rewards specifies a probability kernel $Q$ from $D$ to $S\times[0,1]$; equivalently, each admissible $(s,a)$ has a probability measure $Q(\cdot\mid s,a)$ on that product measurable space. The reward-coordinate projection $(s',\rho)\mapsto\rho$ is measurable because the preimage of each Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$ is the product rectangle $S\times B$. Define the next-state law by $P(s'\mid s,a)=Q(\{s'\}\times[0,1]\mid s,a)$ and the mean reward by $r(s,a)=\int_{S\times[0,1]}\rho\,Q(ds',d\rho\mid s,a)\in[0,1]$. At each time, conditional on the observed history and the selected action, the next-state/reward pair has this law. Assume the Axiom of Choice for the path-space construction under policies.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the policy path laws used in the expectations below. For a finite MDP with bounded rewards, a policy assigns a probability distribution on $A(s)$ to each finite observed history ending in state $s$, with each action probability a measurable function of the history; deterministic policies are included. For states $x,y$, start at $S_0=x$ and define $\tau_y=\inf\{t\ge0:S_t=y\}$, with $\tau_y=+\infty$ if $y$ is never hit. This is an extended nonnegative measurable random variable because $\{\tau_y\le n\}=\bigcup_{t=0}^n\{S_t=y\}$. Take the expectation and the infimum over policies in $[0,+\infty]$. The MDP is communicating if $\inf_\pi\mathbb E_x^\pi[\tau_y]<\infty$ for every ordered pair $(x,y)$. Its raw diameter is $D_0=\sup_{x,y}\inf_\pi\mathbb E_x^\pi[\tau_y]$ in $[0,+\infty]$, and its normalized diameter is $D=\max\{1,D_0\}$ in the extended order. Since $S$ is finite, $D_0$ is finite for every communicating MDP. Thus a one-state MDP has $D_0=0$ and $D=1$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

A chosen real $\mathcal G$-measurable representative is a **version**. Equalities and inequalities involving these classes mean almost-sure equalities and inequalities.

Existence is [[thm-conditional-expectation-exists-by-radon-nikodym]] and uniqueness is [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]], applied to [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$

derivations.claim: Set $V_0(s)=0$ for every state. Backward induction over the finite horizon gives the Bellman recurrence $$V_{n+1}(s)=\max_{a\in A(s)}\left[r(s,a)+\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)V_n(s')\right].$$ For the induction step, suppose that from every state the $n$-step supremum is attained by a deterministic Markov policy and equals $V_n$. Any history-dependent $(n+1)$-step policy may randomize its first action and may condition later actions on the first reward as well as the next state. Conditional on a first action $a$ and one-step outcome $(s',\rho)$, its continuation has expected reward at most $V_n(s')$ by the induction hypothesis, which is independent of the earlier history and reward. Thus its total expected reward is at most $r(s,a)+\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,a)V_n(s')$, averaged over its first-action distribution, and this average is at most the displayed maximum. A maximizing action exists because $A(s)$ is finite; choosing it and then using an attaining $n$-step policy from each possible next state attains equality. The base case $V_0=0$ is attained by the empty policy. This proves both the recurrence and that history dependence cannot improve $V_n$; the joint reward/next-state law is handled by its mean reward and next-state marginal. For any $0\le j\le n$, splitting an $n$-step policy into its first $n-j$ and last $j$ rewards gives $V_n(y)\le V_{n-j}(y)+j$: the first part is at most the optimal $(n-j)$-step value and the last part is at most $j$ because rewards lie in $[0,1]$. For any $x,y$ and $\varepsilon>0$, [F2] gives a policy from $x$ whose hitting time $\tau_y$ has expectation at most $D_0+\varepsilon$. Follow it until $y$ is hit, then use an optimal policy for the remaining $n-\tau_y$ steps if $\tau_y\le n$. On $\{\tau_y=j\}$ for each $0\le j\le n$, the conditional expected total reward given the history through time $j$ is at least $V_{n-j}(y)\ge V_n(y)-j$, since pre-hit rewards are nonnegative. On $\tau_y>n$, the total reward is nonnegative and $V_n(y)\le n<\tau_y$. Summing over the hitting-time events and taking expectations using [F5]–[F8] gives $V_n(x)\ge V_n(y)-\mathbb E[\tau_y]\ge V_n(y)-D_0-\varepsilon$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ and interchanging $x,y$ proves $\max_s V_n(s)-\min_s V_n(s)\le D_0$.

Put $a_n=\max_s V_n(s)$; the maximum exists because $S$ is finite, and $0\le a_n\le n$ by [F1,F8]. For any $(m+n)$-step policy from $s$, the expected first $m$ rewards are at most $V_m(s)$, while conditional on the complete history through state $S_m$ the remaining $n$-step rule is an admissible policy from $S_m$ and its conditional expected reward is at most $V_n(S_m)\le a_n$. By [F4,F5,F6,F7], the unconditional expected total is therefore at most $V_m(s)+a_n\le a_m+a_n$, so $a_{m+n}\le a_m+a_n$. Conversely, choose $s_*$ attaining $a_m$ and use an optimal $m$-step policy from it; after observing $S_m=z$, continue with an optimal $n$-step policy from $z$. By step 1.1, $V_n(z)\ge a_n-D_0$ for every $z$, so [F4,F6,F7] give total expected reward at least $a_m+a_n-D_0$. Hence $a_{m+n}\ge a_m+a_n-D_0$, and $|a_{m+n}-a_m-a_n|\le D_0$.

Apply [F3] to $(a_n)$ with $C=D_0$ to obtain $a_n/n\to\rho^*$ for some finite $\rho^*$. Step 1.1 gives $a_n-D_0\le V_n(s)\le a_n$ for every $s$, so division by $n$ proves $V_n(s)/n\to\rho^*$ for every state. The bounds $0\le V_n(s)\le n$ imply $\rho^*\in[0,1]$.

If $\epsilon\ge V_{\max}$, then $V^*(s)-\epsilon\le0$ for every state and every continuation value is nonnegative, so no time is counted. Assume now $\epsilon<V_{\max}$. The stated $\eta$ satisfies $0<\eta<V_{\max}/4$ and $\eta(1-\gamma)<1$. Apply [F1] with confidence parameter $\delta/2$; its sample threshold is exactly the displayed $m$. On its event, R-MAX has the hypotheses of [F2] with $\zeta=(m+1)|E_\eta|$.

For the uninformative heuristic, $|E_\eta|\le SA$ and $V_{\max}=(1-\gamma)^{-1}$. The displayed $b$ gives $m=O((S+\ln(SA/\delta))V_{\max}^2/[\eta^2(1-\gamma)^2])$. Also $H=O((1-\gamma)^{-1}\ln(1/[\eta(1-\gamma)]))$, since $-\ln\gamma\ge1-\gamma$ for $0<\gamma<1$, and $M=O((V_{\max}/\eta)(\zeta+\ln(2/\delta)))$. Using $\zeta\le(m+1)SA$ and $\eta=\epsilon/4$ yields $\widetilde O(S^2A/[\epsilon^3(1-\gamma)^6])$.
Take $\rho=\delta/2$ in [F2]. Since $4\eta=\epsilon$, the theorem gives $\mathbb P(N_\epsilon\le HM)\ge1-\delta$.

Put $\bar V=(1-\gamma)^{-1}$. Since $V_{\max}\le\bar V$ and $|E_\eta|\le SA$, the instance parameters satisfy $b\ge\bar b$, $m\le\bar m$, $\zeta\le\bar\zeta$, and $q\ge\bar q$, while the truncation horizon is $H=\bar H$. If $\epsilon<V_{\max}$, then $M\le\bar M$ and step 2.1 yields the uniform bound. If $\epsilon\ge V_{\max}$, then $N_\epsilon=0$. Thus the displayed $\bar H\bar M$ is a finite PAC-MDP bound in the sense of the Definition.
